subsubtopic: CLOSURE OF LASER SAILBOAT COMPANY, HAWKESBURY, ONTARIO
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, earlier this year, the world famous Laser Sailboat Company of Hawkesbury, Ontario, was forced into receivership, and closed its doors. In March, the receivers and creditors found a purchaser for the financially beleaguered company.
The purchaser in question, Pearson Yachts, at the urging of the Ontario Development Corporation initially promised to keep 20 to 30 jobs in Canada to build both the Pearson and Laser sailboats.
However, Pearson has now changed its mind and will manufacture all its boats in Portsmouth, Rhode Island. Without a foreign investment review mechanism which this Tory Government cancelled, there appears to be no way to force Laser to stay in Canada much less in Hawkesbury.

subsubtopic: CLOSURE OF LASER SAILBOAT COMPANY, HAWKESBURY, ONTARIO
speechtext: Shame!

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party
subsubtopic: CLOSURE OF LASER SAILBOAT COMPANY, HAWKESBURY, ONTARIO
speechtext: I call upon the Government of Canada to intervene and to set in place mechanisms to keep Laser in Canada. Laser is as Canadian as the Maple Leaf. Let us keep it in Canada, and especially, let us keep it in Hawkesbury.

Mr. Speaker, the practice of drift-net fishing in the North Pacific is one that threatens both the environment we treasure and a salmon resource many British Columbians rely on for their
livelihood. It is estimated that these nets kill at least one million seabirds each year, along with 20,000 porpoises, tens of thousands of seals and a number of whales. Over 30 different species are involved in this eco-system that is being plundered daily by drift-netters.
In addition to the environmental tragedy, it is estimated that between 20,000 and 30,000 tonnes of salmon are caught illegally each year while fishermen drift-net for squid. This has fuelled a thriving salmon industry in southeast Asia, where a tin of sockeye can sell for half the price it does in B.C. When only half of the 30 million pink salmon expected to return to B.C. rivers actually make it, it is not difficult to see that a tremendous problem exists. In order to get maximum benefit from the tremendous job the Government has done in the area of salmonid enhancement, we should start getting tough with the nation showing a reckless attitude towards our environment, while taking a resource that rightfully belongs to Canada.
Hear, hear!

speechtext:

subsubtopic: EFFECT OF GATT DECISION ON SUBSIDIES TO DAIRY FARMERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 31 to express my dismay about the Government's betrayal of our Canadian dairy industry at the mid-term review of multilateral trade negotiations of GATT concluded in Geneva this month. Not only have subsidies and returns been frozen but the dairy industry itself has been under attack from a U.S. challenge to the inclusion of icecream and yogurt on the Import Control List. If this challenge is successful it will have a devastating impact on other sectors of the agriculture economy because of the precedent that it will set.
April 26, 1989

I ask the Government to stand up to the United States negotiators and to expose the hidden, indirect subsidies that are available to their farmers through feed companies, grain elevators, fertilizer companies, et cetera.
For example, a dairy farmer in St. Clair County, Michigan with 44 cows will receive approximately $10,000 worth of subsidies in the form of feed. A wheat farmer with 40 acres of wheat will receive three tonnes of ammonium-nitrate fertilizer, all paid for by the United States Treasury.
This is not a level playing field but a massive erosion of the most sophisticated marketing system of any country in the world. We lost our two-price wheat system. The Government took oats from under the jurisdiction of the Canadian Wheat Board. We are losing our wine industry, and now dairy and poultry are being challenged through GATT.
I call on the Government to promote and to strengthen the Canadian farmers who supply our Canadian consumers with a continuing supply of high quality food.

Mr. Speaker, a delegation from Canada will be in Morocco July 8 to 22 for the first Francophone Games. The delegation will be in three distinct parts: Canada, Canada-Quebec and Canada-New Brunswick. This formula recognizes Canada's traditional participation as a single entity in the French-speaking world and international games, as well as the presence and special recognized contribution of Quebec and New Brunswick in the Francophone community and its institutions.
Mr. Speaker, I repeat the words of Quebec's International Affairs Minister, Paul Gobeil, who says he is satisfied with the agreement because it allows Quebec to keep its place in the French-speaking world and it shows other nations that we are a united country where Quebec, a Canadian province, has a place within the Canadian federation.

subsubtopic: LANDING AND INSPECTION REGULATIONS-ALLEGED LOSS OF JOBS IN B.C.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on behalf of the federal New Democrat caucus I move for the removal of the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Siddon) from Cabinet for failing to bring forward regulations which would have saved the B.C. fishing industry.
The landing and inspection regulations which were brought forward by the Minister will lead to the wholesale exportation of the herring and salmon industry worth $750 million, and will cost us thousands of jobs in B.C.
In the absence of Canadian grading and gutting rights, foreign buyers will intercept B.C. salmon and herring when they are landed. Canada's sovereign rights have been trampled and British Columbians will be the losers.
We point to the fatal flaw in Chapter 12 of the Free Trade Agreement wherein Article 1203 gives protection to the fishing regulations of Quebec, P.E.I., Nova Scotia, Newfoundland and New Brunswick-but not to B.C.
The new Conservative regulations will see foreign buyers snapping up B.C. fish prior to proper grading and processing. While B.C. presently leads world markets in price and quality, the new regulations open the door to low-quality grading and processing outside the B.C. industry.
Up to 7,500 jobs are at risk. Entire coastal communities are placed at economic risk. An entire industry could collapse from the piranha-like activity of foreign buyers-

My question pertains to a commitment made by the Government of Canada in the fall of 1987, following a GATT ruling on the West Coast fishery in which the then Minister of Fisheries made the following promise to me in the House about fish processing jobs: "Fish processing jobs are not going to be jeopardized in any way". April 26, 1989	COMMONS DEBATES	967

speakeroldname: Hon. Gilles Loiselle (Minister of State (Finance)) moved
speechtext:
that Bill C-9, an Act to amend the Bank Act, be read the second time and referred to a Legislative Committee.
He said: Mr. Speaker, on April 13 last I had the honour of tabling the Government's Bill to enhance the service charge disclosure provisions of the Bank Act. Unlike the predecessor Bill, which applied only to personal accounts, Bill C-9 applies to both business and personal accounts on deposit at chartered banks. This policy was developed in co-operation with the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Valcourt) and incorporates measures proposed in consultation with small business and bank representatives. It also responds to many of the recommendations put forth by the Standing Committee on Finance and Economic Affairs. The committee helped focus attention on changes in the
Bank Act
banking industry that left many Canadians surprised by unexpected service charges.

Mr. Speaker, the changes provided in Bill C-9 are based on four premises: first, individuals and companies must be able to make enlightened decisions and compare prices to choose the accounts and institutions that best meet their needs; second, Canadians are entitled to receive reasonable advance notice before new or additional charges are imposed on their deposit accounts; third, customers wishing to complain about service charges must know that a mechanism for this exists both within the bank and with the Government and that they can have access to it.
Competition, not regulation is the best way to guarantee a fair and reasonable approach to establishing prices.
By applying these principles to the Bill, we have made substantial progress towards increasing consumer protection. The provisions of Bill C-9 represent a considerable improvement in the standards to be observed by banks with respect to notice and disclosure of charges to their customers in Canada.

First, in deciding where to do their banking, consumers will be in the best position ever to shop around. Each bank will be required to make available brochures of service charges for their various accounts. A brochure will be available for personal accounts and for business accounts. With such information readily available, consumers will be in a position to choose accounts and institutions that best meet their needs. In addition, for all other kinds of charges, where standard ones exist, the public will have access to a list of all such charges. This requirement, which was one of the major objectives of small business groups, represents a substantial improvement over the previous Bill.
A second major area of enhanced disclosure takes place when a customer chooses his or her accounts.

New customers will first receive a copy of the agreement they have signed, a list of all service charges applicable to their type of account, information respecting the bank's procedures for notifying them of any increase in charges, and information on the bank's procedures relating to complaints.

April 26, 1989
Bank Act
Finally, Mr. Speaker, the situation with respect to changes in related charges has also improved. The bank may not introduce any changes in the charges it applies to a customer's account without giving the customer 30 day's notice. Customers who have accounts with passbooks and, as a result, do not receive monthly statements in the mail, will be advised at least 60 days in advance of any changes in charges by means of signs posted in full view at their branches.
The provisions of this Bill also allow for the fact that in recent years, there has been a increasing tendency among Canadians to use automatic tellers. As a result, banks will have to notify their customers at these outlets of any changes in the charges applied to their accounts.
I would now like to discuss the second major objective of this Bill, which is to provide for complaint mechanisms.
For the first time, banks are obliged to establish a procedure for dealing with customer complaints and to have such procedures approved by the Office of the Superintendent of Financial Institutions.
The banks will also have to designate an administrator or employee who will be responsible for implementing the general complaints procedure and to appoint at least one employee who will receive complaints from the public. Finally, banks will also have to post a notice to inform customers of their right to file complaints with the Office of the Superintendent of Financial Institutions, if the banks are unable to deal with the problem themselves. The name, address and telephone number of the resource person at the Office will also be posted.

This Government continues to monitor service charge practices and is ensuring that Canadians are able to resolve their account-related problems. As part of that process and to ensure that Parliament has the opportunity to assess on an ongoing basis the success of our efforts, the Superintendent will be preparing annual reports on complaints and a report which will be tabled in Parliament. Penalties for non-compliance have also been increased. At present, penalties for breach of the disclosure provisions are to a maximum of $1,000. This new legislation provides for a maximum penalty of $500,000 for a breach of any of the provisions without reasonable cause. There may be some who say we should have gone further in regulating charges. To this I respond first, that as a matter of principle this Government is not in favour
of price regulation, particularly in markets where there is competition.
This Bill represents a reasonable and responsible approach to the major issues. Through this Bill, consumers and business will have assurances about the treatment they will receive from banks. Banks, too, will understand their role and responsibility in serving their customers.
Moreover, the Government will shortly be bringing forth its legislation on financial institutions reform which, by breaking down barriers, will foster an even more competitive environment.

In concluding, Mr. Speaker, I would like to add the following clarification. Once implemented, the Bill and the measures taken last year by the banks with respect to basic charges and accounts will make it possible to deal with concerns expressed by many Canadians before the Finance Committee of the House of Commons.
From now on, as soon as they open an account, Canadians will be informed of the charges involved and of their rights. They will be advised of any changes in the charge schedule, in a manner that is far more acceptable than was the case before.
They will also have direct access to a complaint settlement mechanism, first at their bank, and if they do not obtain satisfaction, at the Office of the Superintendent of Financial Institutions which will act as a mediator.
Mr. Speaker, we are convinced that these measures will help consumers and companies to get the most out of their financial institutions and that the industry will become more competitive.
